title: BANG under counter-attack, 19 September 1944
eyebrow: East of Formosa · BANG's third war patrol · convoy TAKA-909's escorts

participants.name: CD-30
participants.note: kaibokan; the hunt's leader in the 4th Surface Escort Division's order (W-15's diary p57)

participants.name: Taian Maru
participants.note: auxiliary escort, with CD-30 in the escort division's summary (p12)

paras.text: The hunt after BANG's attacks on convoy TAKA-909: eleven and a half hours from her going deep to her surfacing, about 80 depth charges by her count, and the escorts' claim of a submarine sunk, set beside her depth log in the water she was in.

BANG survived without recorded damage. Her report: "Very deliberate depth charging began 4 minutes after firing. Three escorts ... let us have about 80 charges in patterns of 3 6 or 9 during the next 4½ hours. We were running silent at 450 feet under a 24 degree negative gradient" (p. 7) [[cite:rg38-74802831/p07]]. The Japanese record: CD-30 and Taian Maru, with aircraft, attacked the submarine at 24-54N 122-23E, "one enemy submarine sunk" (the 4th Surface Escort Division's daily summary, p. 12) [[cite:jacar:C08030144100]].

BANG fired at 0915 K and went straight to 400 feet, having seen an escort at about 2,000 yards with a zero angle on the bow; she was at 450 feet by 0920 K. On the Japanese side, at 0938 I (0838 K) the 4th Surface Escort Division ordered a 4th Sweep Unit, aircraft of the Okinawa Air Group and two of the convoy's escorts chosen by CD-30's captain, "to destroy the enemy submarine that torpedoed No. 2 Tosei Maru" (W-15's diary, p. 57) [[cite:jacar:C08030607800]]: the order came an hour after the escorts had begun. W-15 left the convoy off Keelung at 1256 I, reached the scene at 1625 I and joined CD-30; at 1630 I it received the report that CD-30, with aircraft, had certainly sunk the submarine, and broke off at 1700 (p. 53). BANG came to periscope depth at 1730 K, the same minute as that report (1630 I), with nothing in sight, and surfaced at 2050 K.

sections.heading: The escorts' doctrine, as their officers gave it after the war

paras.text: What the Japanese officers told the Naval Technical Mission in 1945 (report S-24) fits what BANG heard. An escort ran in on the echo at 12 knots, went to 16 knots at 800 meters and dropped on the time its chemical recorder gave; "The Japanese had no means of determining the depth of enemy submarines, and their depth charge patterns were designed to cover all depths"; small patterns went on doubtful contacts, the largest on sure ones (p. 11). The deepest setting usually carried was 120 meters, about 394 ft, "and a proportionate number of charges with this setting was included in each pattern" (p. 12) [[cite:ntmj-s24:p12]]: at 450 ft BANG was below the deepest of them. Having lost contact, an escort ran on about 1,000 meters, reversed to the right, skirted the turbulent water at about 500 meters, came back through the point of contact, stopped and listened; several escorts took successive runs, each stopping to listen while the next attacked (pp. 13-15). That is "very deliberate depth charging" over four and a half hours. A claimed kill was judged first by "Oil and the length of time it continued to come up" (p. 45) [[cite:ntmj-s24:p45]], which is what CD-30 and the aircraft reported.

The water column is drawn to scale: BANG's silhouette at her logged depth, the Japanese pistols' depth settings as War Damage Report 58 gives them, the layer from her bathythermograph card of that evening (isothermal to 120 ft, a gradient to 450 ft), and the seafloor under her track. Where any charge burst is not recorded. The inner ring round each setting is the Bureau's distance for pressure hull rupture of a boat of her class (SS-285 on: a 7/8-inch high tensile steel hull) at the Type 2's 357 lb, about 23 ft, read off its figure 15-2, which holds "for shallow submergence condition only" [[cite:wdr58:15/fig15-2]]; the outer rings are its bands of serious and of moderate damage, 50 and 100 ft [[cite:wdr58:15/15-12]]. An illustration of the scale, not a placement. The deepest setting the Type 95 could take was 292 ft and the deepest normally used on the Type 2 was 390 ft (paragraph 3-12) [[cite:wdr58:3/3-12]]: at 450 ft BANG was below both. The explainer, *Depth charges*, works through the rest.
BANG kept zone K (−10); the Japanese records Tokyo time (I, −9).

CD-30's own diary or action report, with the charges it dropped and their settings: not on JACAR (searched 11-12 Nov 2026, with the Navy's telegram file of 1944-45). Which aircraft flew. Where any charge went off.

BANG's third war patrol report, NARA microfilm M1752 (74802831), with its depth log and bathythermograph card. The 4th Surface Escort Division's war diary and minesweeper W-15's war diary, September 1944, via JACAR (C08030144100, C08030607800). BuShips War Damage Report No. 58 (1949), an assessment after the war. Seafloor: NOAA ETOPO1 under her track.

events.translation: Separate sheet 1. (1) 0820: at E 122°23′ N 24°52′, No. 7 ship Tosei Maru torpedoed. (2) 0830: W-15 leads the convoy back to Keelung. (3) 1256: off Keelung island, leaves the convoy for the scene. (4) 1625: arrives; begins attacking the enemy submarine with CD-30. (5) 1630: receives the report that CD-30, working with aircraft, has certainly sunk the enemy submarine. (6) 1700: breaks off the search for Keelung. (7) 2000: anchors at Keelung
events.note: Minesweeper W-15's war diary, September 1944 (第十五號掃海艇戦時日誌, cover p42; the ship written 東勢丸, without the 第二 of J02 and J04), the 19th's action written up on a separate sheet as the daily page (p49) says. W-15 was one of TAKA-909's six escorts (J06). Its daily page: 0210 sailed escorting TAKA-909 for Naha; 0830 Tosei Maru torpedoed; 2000 anchored at Keelung. Five minutes after BANG's Attacks 3-4 (0915 K = 0815 I), 8 nm east-south-east of her position (24-56N 122-14.5E), and the first record with a time and place for the sinking: J02 has the place but no time, J04's 0925 is 65 minutes later. The convoy put back to Keelung, so the escort's own diary answers the question J06 left open. The 1630 report of a submarine certainly sunk "with aircraft" has the same time and wording (撃沈確實) as the Navy summary's entry for the 953rd Air Group, which the summary puts on the 20th (J05): possibly the same event, dated a day later there. BANG was at 450 ft from 0920 K and came to periscope depth at 1730 K (1630 I) with nothing in sight

events.translation: 4th Surface Escort Division signal operations order No. 89: the 4th Sweep Unit (formed of aircraft the commander of the Okinawa Air Group designates and two ships of the TAKA-909 force that CD-30's captain designates) is to destroy the enemy submarine that torpedoed No. 2 Tosei Maru at N 24°54′ E 122°23′
events.note: Minesweeper W-15's war diary, September 1944, 三 令達報告等 (orders and reports), the order's row: from the 4th Surface Escort Division's commander, 19th 0938; to CD-30's captain, W-15's captain and the Okinawa Air Group's commander (以下省略, the rest left out), 19th 1055 (read as the time received). Read at 170 dpi. The hunt that BANG heard as "very deliberate depth charging" from 0920 K (0820 I) was by then 78 minutes old: the order names it after the fact and gives it aircraft. The two ships are CD-30 and Taian Maru (J02). It names the Okinawa Air Group (沖空), where J02 has "army aircraft"; which aircraft flew is not found (searched: the 901st Air Group's Oroku detachment, which served under the Okinawa Air Group, September 1944, jacar:C13120411700 p07: its five sorties of the 19th were over a convoy 25 minutes from Naha, not here; the 953rd Air Group's Tamsui detachment, jacar:C13120418300 p24: four seaplanes on convoy escort and one on anti-submarine escort on the 19th, nothing entered). CD-30's own war diary is not on JACAR (searched by its name in every form, 11 Nov 2026). Nor is its report in the Navy's telegram file 行動其他電報綴 (jacar:C19010036800, 373 documents, compiled postwar by the Ministry of Health and Welfare's repatriation bureau): its index (jacar:C19010037100, pp1-4, by document number, date received and sender) has no document from September 1944; nearly all are April 1945, and CD-30 (海30) appears once, document 293, 19 April 1945 (12 Nov 2026)

paras.text: Attacked by BANG on 19 September 1944 off the north-east coast of Formosa. The Okinawa diary names six escorts and the one ship lost, No. 2 Tosei Maru, and says CD-30 and Taian Maru with army aircraft attacked the submarine and claimed it sunk. BANG surfaced that night after about 80 depth charges.

**Route and size** from the 4th Surface Escort Division's table of convoys given air cover (jacar:C08030144100 p05, read on the image 5 Nov 2026): on the 19th, TAKA-909, ten ships of 34,049 tons, escorted by CD-30, W-15, No. 3 Takunan Maru, Shichiri Maru, Taian Maru and No. 3 Taihei Maru, routed Keelung to Kagoshima and Naha to Kagoshima. So it sailed from Keelung, not Takao as the convoy code had suggested. Its sailing time and cargo are not recorded. The waypoints off Formosa's east coast and Kagoshima Bay are assumed. BANG counted eight merchantmen, one an oiler.

No other US boat's attack on TAKA-909 has been found: the diary's columns for the 18th–21st have only this attack and, on the 20th, an attack on the depot ship Jingei far to the east (N27-12.5 E127-10.0; not BANG's).

**The escort W-15's diary** (jacar:C08030607800, September 1944, read on the images 11 Nov 2026) gives the voyage: sailed from Keelung for Naha at 0210 on the 19th; No. 7 ship Tosei Maru torpedoed at 0820 at 24-52N 122-23E (p53); W-15 led the convoy back to Keelung, anchoring at 2000. The convoy sailed again at 06?0 on the 20th (noon 25-01N 122-21E), anchored at Miyako at 1530 on the 21st (noon 24-51.5N 124-45E), sailed again that evening, and dispersed off Naha at 1350 on the 23rd, W-15 entering at 1520 (p49-p50). No attack is entered for the night of the 20th, when BANG fired at a convoy east of Keelung (engagement `bang-east-of-formosa-1944-09-20`). Times I.
To find: TAKA-909's ships' names and cargo (CD-30's or the other escorts' September diaries, not found on JACAR).
